title: Alpha-helix structural modeling
research_question: What polypeptide-chain configurations satisfy known chemical-bond geometry and hydrogen-bonding constraints?
context: A structural chemistry problem later published with Robert B. Corey and H. R. Branson in 1951.
known_at_the_time: Chemical-bond lengths, angles, peptide-group geometry and hydrogen-bonding constraints could restrict admissible polypeptide structures.
X-ray diffraction evidence existed for fibrous proteins, but interpretation was incomplete.
unknown_at_the_time: The later breadth of alpha-helix occurrence across protein structures.
trigger_or_anomaly: The global protein-structure problem had many possible configurations, motivating use of strong local chemical constraints to reduce the search space.
decision_action: Use known local chemical geometry and hydrogen-bonding constraints to construct precise candidate helical configurations rather than freely fitting a global shape.
observed_result: The 1951 publication proposed hydrogen-bonded helical configurations; the alpha helix became a foundational protein structural motif.
alternative_interpretations: The success cannot be attributed to a single heuristic alone; theoretical chemistry, collaboration, model-building skill and available experimental evidence all contributed.
